title: Overmanaged and Underled
subtitle: Leadership & Compliance Orientation Study — OMAC International
description: This study examines how healthcare organizations balance standards compliance with clinical leadership. Your responses are anonymous and used for research purposes only. The instrument takes approximately 6–8 minutes to complete.

questions.label: Current role
Years of experience in healthcare quality or patient safety
Sector
Accreditation/certification held by your organization
Number of accreditation/certification cycles your organization has completed
Time elapsed since your organization's last full accreditation survey/audit
In my organization, leadership treats accreditation standards as a foundation to keep improving on, not a finish line.
After we pass a survey/audit, leadership continues to invest time in strengthening the processes involved.
Leaders in my organization actively look for ways standards can be adapted to improve patient care, beyond minimum compliance.
Leadership revisits and updates protocols even when there is no upcoming survey/audit.
My organization's leaders treat accreditation as an ongoing commitment rather than a one-time achievement.
Once accreditation/certification is achieved, leadership attention to the relevant processes noticeably decreases.
In my organization, passing the survey/audit is treated as the main goal, rather than a step toward better care.
Leadership involvement in standards-related activities is highest just before a survey/audit and drops off afterward.
My organization's leaders view compliance primarily as risk avoidance rather than improvement.
Once a standard is "checked off," it rarely gets revisited by leadership.
Staff in my department often complete checklists/protocols without fully engaging with their purpose.
Documentation of compliance sometimes happens even when the actual step was not meaningfully performed.
Checklist or protocol use in my department is treated as a formality rather than a safety practice.
Under time pressure, staff prioritize completing the paperwork over the substance of the check.
I have observed compliance activities becoming "tick-box" exercises over time.
Leaders in my organization clearly communicate a vision for improving quality beyond minimum requirements.
Leadership actively aligns staff across departments toward shared quality-improvement goals.
Leaders in my organization encourage staff to challenge existing processes when they no longer serve patient safety.
My organization's leadership initiates meaningful change even when current processes are technically compliant.
Leadership in my organization motivates staff to go beyond compliance toward genuine improvement.
When problems are identified, leadership acts on them proactively rather than waiting for the next audit cycle.
